The v6 theorem promises \(w_k(t)=\widehat w_k\log t+\rho_k(t)\), with bounded \(\rho_k(t)\), for almost all separable multiclass datasets. In v7, Theorem 7 requires vectors \(\widetilde w_k\) satisfying
\[\eta\exp\!\left[-x_n^\top(\widetilde w_{y_n}-\widetilde w_k)\right]=\alpha_{n,k}\qquad(k\in[K],\ n\in S_k),\]

checks.location: Abstract headline agreement versus Tables 6 and 24
checks.claim: Mean trajectory-only judge agreement is 84.1 percent across the three API models.
checks.explanation: The displayed table means differ from 84.1%, but the headline does not explicitly identify itself as either mean. A weighted per-example interpretation is possible and cannot be evaluated without the judge cohort counts.
checks.demonstration:
The abstract and introduction report 84.1% agreement for trajectory-only judging across three API models. They do not define that number as an arithmetic mean of the displayed model averages. Table 6 labels its metric as agreement with reference correctness and prints model averages of 76.7%, 79.3%, and 78.2%. Their unweighted mean is

$$\frac{76.7+79.3+78.2}{3}=\frac{1171}{15}\%\approx78.0667\%.$$

Table 24 gives 16 dataset cells for each model. Averaging all 48 displayed SoT-Judge cells equally yields

$$A=\frac{9119}{120}\%\approx75.9917\%.$$

Neither computation yields 84.1%, and no SoT-Judge cell in those two tables equals 84.1%. Section 4.2 explains differences against baselines using the Table 6 averages, but it does not connect the headline number to the same averaging rule or cohort. Appendix E defines the judge and its inputs without specifying the headline's evaluation weights. The released judge evaluator computes per-example correctness agreement, whereas the pinned public result manifest supplies no judge record counts or judge aggregate capable of reconstructing this headline.

A different weighting is mathematically possible. Let $a_1,\ldots,a_{48}$ be the Table 24 percentages, choose a cell with $a_j=100$, and put

$$\lambda=\frac{84.1-A}{100-A}=\frac{973}{2881},\qquad w_i=\frac{1-\lambda}{48}+\lambda\,\mathbf1\{i=j\}.$$

All weights are strictly positive, they sum to one, and $\sum_iw_i a_i=84.1$. Rational weights can be realized by integer cohort-size ratios after multiplication by a common denominator. This is a possible interpretation, not a reconstruction of the authors' experiment. It demonstrates why the table arithmetic cannot establish that the headline is false without first identifying the evaluation cohort and aggregation rule.

The original allegation therefore remains unverified. The available evidence establishes that the ordinary table averages differ from the headline; it does not establish which quantity the headline summarizes. A scientific error grade would require that missing connection.
checks.repair:
First identify the evaluation cohort and the weights attached to datasets and models. If the intended headline is the equal-model mean of the Table 6 averages, the supported value is approximately 78.1%. If it is the equal-dataset mean of the 48 Table 24 cells, the supported value is approximately 76.0%. Rounding to one decimal place cannot turn either into 84.1%.

For a pooled per-example agreement, let $n_{md}$ be the number of judged examples for model $m$ and dataset $d$, and let $c_{md}$ be the number whose predicted correctness agrees with the reference. The quantity to reproduce is

$$100\,\frac{\sum_{m,d}c_{md}}{\sum_{m,d}n_{md}}\%,\qquad 0\le c_{md}\le n_{md}.$$

Supplying those counts, the precise inclusion rules, and any train/test filtering would make the 84.1% claim checkable. If that calculation yields 84.1%, the headline needs an explicit metric definition rather than a numerical correction. Until then, changing 84.1% to either table mean would select an estimand that the source has not specified.

checks.claim: Type-I error of T = 1{|mu_hat/sigma_hat| >= 5 sqrt(L/(n alpha_n))} is <= delta via the union of {|mu_hat|/sigma >= 10 sqrt(L/n)} and {sigma_hat^2/sigma^2 <= alpha_n/4}.
checks.explanation: On the scale event used in the proof, rejection at the printed threshold only implies \(\lvert\widehat\mu\rvert>2.5\sigma r\). The mean-estimation premise controls errors beyond \(10\sigma r\). The two events in the displayed union therefore need not contain the rejection event.
checks.demonstration:
Under the null \(\mu=0\), the complement of the lower-tail scale event gives
\[\widehat\sigma>\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_n}}2\sigma.\]
Rejection then gives only
\[\lvert\widehat\mu\rvert\ge\frac{5\widehat\sigma r}{\sqrt{\alpha_n}}>\frac52\sigma r,\]
which does not imply the mean-error event used in the proof.

For a concrete failure of the event inclusion, take \(\alpha_n=\sigma=1\) and an outcome with \(\widehat\sigma=3/5\) and \(\widehat\mu=4r\). The test rejects because \(4r\ge3r\), while
\[4r<10r,\qquad \widehat\sigma^2=\frac9{25}>\frac14.\]
Neither event on the right occurs. This disproves the displayed set inclusion; it is a counterexample to that inference, not a distributional counterexample to every median-of-means mean estimator. The same calculation shows that the stated interval radius can be only \(2.5\sigma r\) when its supplied mean-error bound is \(10\sigma r\).
checks.repair:
Assume valid estimator guarantees
\[\Pr\!\left(\lvert\widehat\mu-\mu\rvert>10\sigma r\right)\le\frac\delta2,\qquad \Pr\!\left(\widehat\sigma\notin\left[\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_n}}2\sigma,\sqrt{10}\sigma\right]\right)\le\frac\delta2.\]
Use the closed interval
\[\left[\widehat\mu-\frac{20\widehat\sigma r}{\sqrt{\alpha_n}},\ \widehat\mu+\frac{20\widehat\sigma r}{\sqrt{\alpha_n}}\right].\]
On the intersection of the two good events, its radius is at least \(10\sigma r\), so it contains \(\mu\). The union bound gives coverage at least \(1-\delta\), without an independence assumption. Its dual test rejects when \(\lvert\widehat\mu\rvert>20\widehat\sigma r/\sqrt{\alpha_n}\); the strict inequality handles boundary atoms.

For the Type II bound, \(\lvert\mu\rvert\ge74\sigma r/\sqrt{\alpha_n}\) gives, on the same good events,
\[\lvert\widehat\mu\rvert\ge\lvert\mu\rvert-10\sigma r\ge\frac{64\sigma r}{\sqrt{\alpha_n}}>\frac{20\sqrt{10}\sigma r}{\sqrt{\alpha_n}}\ge\frac{20\widehat\sigma r}{\sqrt{\alpha_n}}.\]
Thus Type II error is at most \(\delta\) as well. These are conditional repairs of the test and interval constants; the scale premise itself fails for the paper's proposed estimator, as shown in the separate variance-estimator issue.
checks.scope: The invalid step is the Type I union bound in Appendix A.2 and the corresponding radius in Section 4.2. Changing the constants repairs this inference when the stated mean and scale bounds hold. It does not repair Proposition 4.1 or establish the upper bound of Theorem 2.1(i) for the original distribution class.
checks.title: The test threshold is too small for the stated estimator bounds
checks.claimContext: Write \(L=\log(1/\delta)\), \(r=\sqrt{L/n}\), and \(0<\alpha_n\le1\). Appendix A.2 assumes a mean error at most \(10\sigma r\) and a scale estimate between \(\sqrt{\alpha_n}\sigma/2\) and \(\sqrt{10}\sigma\). It claims that the test with threshold \(5\widehat\sigma r/\sqrt{\alpha_n}\) has Type I error at most \(\delta\). Section 4.2 uses the same constant as an interval radius.

checks.location: Prop. 4.1 (Sec. 4.1) and its proof, App. A.3 'Lower bound'; consequently Sec. 4.2 interval and the upper bound of Thm 2.1(i)/Prop. 3.2
checks.claim: Prop. 4.1: for P_xi in P_{alpha_n}(n,delta), n alpha_n >= C L and K = C log(1/delta), the MoM variance estimator satisfies alpha_n/4 <= sigma_hat^2/sigma^2 <= 10 w.p. >= 1-delta/2; hence the Sec. 4.2 interval covers mu w.p. >= 1-delta (upper bound of Thm 2.1).
checks.explanation: The effective-mass definition permits a rare atom to carry nearly all the variance. Most blocks can miss that atom even when the effective-mass parameter equals one. Their median second moment can then be too small even with the true mean as center. With a valid median-of-means center, the stated confidence interval can have zero width away from the true mean.
checks.demonstration:
Write \(L=\log(1/\delta)\) and choose \(p=1.01L/n\). Consider iid observations from the two-point law
\[X=\begin{cases}-\sqrt{p/(1-p)},&\text{with probability }1-p,\\ \sqrt{(1-p)/p},&\text{with probability }p.\end{cases}\]
The two contributions to \(\mathbb EX\) cancel, and
\[\mathbb EX^2=(1-p)\frac p{1-p}+p\frac{1-p}p=1.\]
Thus \(\mu=0\) and \(\sigma^2=1\). For sufficiently large \(n/L\), both squared support values are at most \(n/L\), giving the paper's actual supremum parameter \(\alpha_{n,\delta}=1\). The sample ratio \(n/L\) can be arbitrarily large, so the required \(n\alpha_n=\Omega(L)\) condition causes no obstruction.

First, take the permitted lower parameter \(\alpha_n=1/4\). Truncating at \(n\alpha_n/L\) retains only the smaller atom, whose contribution to the second moment is
\[(1-p)\frac p{1-p}=p<\frac14.\]
This contradicts the proof's inference from the supremum definition. More strongly, the variance estimator fails even at \(\alpha_n=1\), where this truncation objection disappears and the truncated expectation is exactly one.

To see this, use \(K=CL\) equal blocks of size \(m=n/K\), choosing integer-compatible values with \(K\le n/2\). Let \(j=\lfloor K/2\rfloor+1\), and let \(E\) be the event that the first \(j\) blocks contain only the small atom. Independence gives
\[\Pr(E)=(1-p)^{mj}.\]
With the oracle center \(\widehat\mu=0\), which meets Proposition 4.1's centering premise with probability one, each of these blocks has second moment \(p/(1-p)<1/4\). A strict majority therefore forces the median second moment below \(1/4\), under either median convention. For every fixed \(C>0\), choose \(K\) sufficiently large that \(1.01j/K<1\), then take \(n/L\) sufficiently large. Since
\[(1-p)^{mj}\sim \exp(-1.01Lj/K)=\delta^{1.01j/K}>\delta,\]
this event violates the proposition's failure probability. Retuning the fixed block constant does not remove it.

The same law also defeats the actual Section 4.2 interval with a valid estimated center. Use a standard median-of-means center with \(K_\mu=8L\) blocks. A block mean has variance \(8L\sigma^2/n\), so Chebyshev's inequality bounds its probability of error larger than \(10\sigma\sqrt{L/n}\) by \(0.08\). Hoeffding's inequality then gives a median failure probability at most
\[\exp\{-2(8L)(1/2-0.08)^2\}=\exp(-2.8224L)<\delta.\]
This verifies the stipulated mean-estimator premise uniformly over finite-variance laws.

Let \(N\) count rare observations in the whole sample. If \(N<4L\), fewer than half of the \(8L\) mean blocks can contain a rare observation. Their median is consequently the small atom itself, regardless of how the mean and variance partitions overlap. Since \(\mathbb EN=1.01L\), the binomial tail bound gives
\[\Pr(N\ge4L)\le\left(\frac{e\cdot1.01}{4}\right)^{4L}=\delta^{1.505\ldots}.\]
On \(E\cap\{N<4L\}\), the strict majority of clean variance blocks are centered exactly at their common atom. Hence \(\widehat\sigma^2=0\), and the resulting zero-width interval excludes the true mean zero. Its miscoverage probability is at least \(\Pr(E)-\Pr(N\ge4L)\), which exceeds \(\delta\) for sufficiently large \(L\) and \(n/L\).

For the concrete choice \(n=1{,}260{,}000\), \(L=20\), \(K_\mu=160\) and \(K=3000\), this lower bound is
\[4.0801\times10^{-5}-8.4037\times10^{-14},\qquad \delta=2.0612\times10^{-9}.\]
Thus both the block-scale guarantee and the stated interval construction fail inside the claimed distribution class. This argument does not settle the separate existence assertion in Theorem 2.1(i).
checks.repair: The scale premise must be replaced or proved under a stronger distributional assumption that prevents most blocks from missing the variance-carrying component. Changing the fixed block-count constant cannot do this: the clean-majority event in the proof occurs for every fixed \(C>0\), even with the true mean as center. For any alternative scale estimate that does satisfy the stated two-sided bound with failure probability \(\delta/2\), the radius-20 construction in the separate constant issue gives a proved coverage result when the mean estimate also fails with probability at most \(\delta/2\). No alternative scale guarantee for the original effective-mass class is established here.
checks.scope: The contradiction applies to Proposition 4.1 and the Section 4.2 median-of-means interval construction, invalidating the upper-bound proof through that construction. It does not disprove the existence of a different interval satisfying Theorem 2.1(i); that existence assertion remains unresolved.
checks.title: The proposed variance estimator can collapse inside the claimed class
checks.whyItMatters: The variance estimate can collapse on a distribution allowed by the theorem, so the interval built from it can miss the true mean with probability much larger than the stated error level.
checks.claimContext: The paper defines a distribution class through the effective-mass parameter \(\alpha_{n,\delta}\). Proposition 4.1 claims that a median of blockwise second moments estimates the variance from below by \(\alpha_n\sigma^2/4\) and from above by \(10\sigma^2\), with probability at least \(1-\delta/2\). Section 4.2 uses that estimate to set its confidence-interval width.

checks.claim: Algorithm7 achieves exp(−Omega(n)) for all the stated delta and search-horizon choices.
checks.explanation: The advertised range permits noise that dominates the bounded score differences. For a fixed language family and fixed distribution, Algorithm 7 can have a positive error lower bound for every allowed horizon choice. A fixed positive mass floor cannot be used to rescue this broad claim while simultaneously requiring an unbounded window in an infinite supported language.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(\mathcal U=\mathbb N\), let the only supported language be \(L_2=\{1\}\cup\{2k:k\ge2\}\), and give it probabilities \(\Pr(1)=1/2\) and \(\Pr(2k)=2^{-k}\). For each \(i\ne2\), set \(L_i=\{1,3\}\cup\{2k+1:k\ge i+2\}\). This is one fixed countable family; every bad language has unsupported witness \(3\), and every possible output from it beyond threshold \(t\ge1\) is unsupported. Thus the reference index is \(i^*=2\), the witness index is \(3\), and the source’s coverage and witness assumptions hold. Section 2.1 defines generation failure as \(\widehat x\notin\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal D)\setminus S\); selecting any bad language implies this event regardless of the random tail rank.

Choose \(\varepsilon=1/2\) and \(\delta_n=e^{-n^2}\). For any admissible \(f,h,g\), we have \(f\ge2\), \(h\ge6\), and \(g\le np_h^*/2\le n/2\). Every score satisfies \(|q_{i,t}|\le h\), and the algorithm adds independent noise with \[\sigma=\frac hg\frac{\sqrt{fh}}\varepsilon\sqrt{2\log(1.25/\delta_n)}.\] Consequently \(\|q/\sigma\|_2\le1/(4\sqrt2)\), conditional on every sample. The KL divergence between \(\mathcal N(q/\sigma,I)\) and \(\mathcal N(0,I)\) is \(\|q/\sigma\|_2^2/2\); Pinsker therefore bounds their total-variation distance by \(1/(8\sqrt2)\). Under the zero-mean law, the maximal coordinate is uniform and chooses a bad language with probability \(1-1/f\ge1/2\). Hence actual generation error is at least \[\frac12-\frac1{8\sqrt2}>0.41\] for every admissible horizon schedule, including schedules depending on privacy inputs. Nonempty admissible diverging schedules exist, for example \(f=h=\lfloor\log n\rfloor\) and \(g=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\) for sufficiently large \(n\).

The fixed-mass-floor corollary is separate. A fixed \(p_0>0\) cannot bound all positive masses in an infinite reference language when \(h\to\infty\). Under that inherited reading its premise is incompatible, so the growing-window example is not a counterexample within that premise.
checks.repair: Retain Equation (E.13) and state an exponential rate only when its coverage exponent and \(\varepsilon^2g^2/[256fh\log(1.25/\delta)]\), after subtracting their logarithmic prefactors, are both bounded below by \(cn\) for some fixed \(c>0\). For a genuinely fixed witness window with a fixed mass floor and \(g=\Theta(n)\), a sufficient privacy restriction is \(fh\log(1.25/\delta)=O(n)\), with a small enough constant and sublinear log-prefactor. Do not combine a fixed positive floor with a growing window over an infinite language.
checks.scope: The counterexample concerns Algorithm 7 in the explicitly advertised sample-size-dependent privacy range. It does not refute a separate pointwise claim for each fixed \(\delta\) with \(\delta\)-dependent constants and sample thresholds, or an existence theorem for some different private learner. Equation (E.13) remains an upper bound and can become vacuous in this regime.

checks.claim: \text{Var}[\hat{A}^{\text{PRPO}}_{k,i}]\leq\text{Var}[\hat{A}^{\text{GRPO}}_{i}].
checks.explanation:
The proof establishes an inequality for an optimally chosen mixing weight, then applies it to the configured weight. It also treats a more accurate estimate of the reward mean as if it necessarily reduced the variance of a standardized residual. The residual and its random denominator change together, so that inference is invalid.

There is an earlier definition problem: a finite group can contain identical rewards, making its empirical standard deviation zero. The printed estimator does not specify that case. Completing it in either of two common ways still does not give the claimed variance ordering.
checks.demonstration:
Consider four permutation contexts with identical reward laws and five independent rollouts per context, matching $m=4$ and $G=5$. Each rollout receives reward $1$ with probability $0.1$, and reward $0.1$ otherwise. Both values belong to the paper's reward scheme. Set the advantage of a constant group to zero and use the empirical variance with divisor equal to the group size.

Exchangeability gives a particularly simple calculation. A nonconstant standardized group has average squared residual one; a constant group contributes zero. Therefore a fixed local coordinate has variance
$$v_A=1-0.1^5-0.9^5=0.4095,$$
whereas its globally standardized counterpart has variance
$$v_B=1-0.1^{20}-0.9^{20}=0.8784233454.$$
Summing the finite binomial probabilities gives $\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)=0.5385553844$. At the reported local weight $\alpha=0.1$,
$$\operatorname{Var}(0.1A+0.9B)=0.8125578790>0.4095.$$
The inequality also fails with sample-standard-deviation normalization, and with the everywhere-defined denominator $\widehat\sigma+10^{-6}$. These completions are stated explicitly; they are not silently attributed to the manuscript.
checks.repair:
First define the zero-standard-deviation case. Then state the actual condition on the mixing weight using
$$v(\alpha)=\alpha^2v_A+(1-\alpha)^2v_B+2\alpha(1-\alpha)c.$$
When $v_A+v_B-2c>0$, its minimizer on $[0,1]$ is
$$\alpha_* = \operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{v_B-c}{v_A+v_B-2c}\right).$$
Because $\alpha=1$ is feasible, this oracle choice gives $v(\alpha_*)\leq v_A$. If the denominator is zero, $A-B$ is constant and all mixing weights have the same variance. Neither fact proves the configured weight is optimal. A gradient-variance guarantee additionally requires analysis of the advantage multiplied by the policy score.
checks.scope: This concerns the stated variance guarantee, including the configured reward regime under explicit standard completions of the undefined normalizer. It does not establish that every PRPO gradient has larger variance.
checks.claimContext: PRPO combines a locally standardized reward $A$ with a reward $B$ standardized across all permutations: $A_\alpha=\alpha A+(1-\alpha)B$. Theorem A.3 claims that this advantage has no more variance than the local GRPO advantage.
checks.title: Pooling normalized rewards does not guarantee lower variance
checks.whyItMatters: The claimed theoretical explanation for reduced variance needs a condition on the mixing weight and on the estimator, rather than the number of pooled samples alone.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem A.3, variance-reduction proof; two-level advantage definition; Table 4

checks.claim: \mathbb{E}\left[\nabla_{\theta}L^{\text{PRPO}}(\theta)\right]=\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta),
checks.explanation: Zero mean of an advantage does not make its product with the policy score unbiased. The sample mean includes the focal rollout's reward, and the sample standard deviation also depends on that rollout. Both operations change the score–reward covariance. The proof does not calculate this dependence.
checks.demonstration:
Use a three-action softmax policy with probabilities $p=(0.2,0.3,0.5)$ and rewards $r=(0,0.1,1)$. Give both permutation contexts this same policy, take $m=G=2$ and $\alpha=0.1$, and evaluate at a reference policy equal to the current policy. Ratios are then one, clipping is locally inactive, and the KL gradient is zero.

For the logits, the true reward gradient is
$$\nabla J=p\odot(r-p^\top r)=(-0.106,-0.129,0.235).$$
Freeze the sampled advantages when differentiating the surrogate, assign zero advantage to a constant group, and average the four rollout score terms. Exact enumeration of all $3^4=81$ action batches gives
$$\mathbb E[\widehat g]=(-0.193857716,-0.194178930,0.388036646).$$
This vector is not even parallel to $\nabla J$, so a missing overall normalization cannot explain the difference. Sample-standard-deviation normalization gives a different vector with the same nonparallelity. Even removing the random division leaves own-sample centering biased: its expectation is $\tfrac{29}{40}\nabla J$ in this example.
checks.repair:
For an unbiased on-policy reward gradient, average score terms $(R_i-b_i)\nabla\log\pi_\theta(o_i\mid x)$ with a baseline whose conditional expectation is independent of the focal action. A leave-one-out baseline from independent other rollouts has this property. Do not divide by a reward-dependent random standard deviation if the target is the raw reward gradient.

Indeed, conditional on the context and the other rollouts,
$$\mathbb E[b_i\nabla\log\pi_\theta(o_i\mid x)]=b_i\sum_o\nabla\pi_\theta(o\mid x)=0.$$
The remaining reward term is exactly $\nabla J$. Clipping, a different behavior policy, and KL regularization each require their own objective or bias analysis.
checks.scope: The printed zero-standard-deviation case is unspecified; the numerical counterexample explicitly uses a common completion. The error concerns the unbiasedness proof and raw reward-gradient identity.
checks.claimContext: Theorem A.6 identifies the expected PRPO gradient with the gradient of the unregularized expected reward $J(\theta)$. Its proof uses the fact that both normalized advantages are centered.

checks.claim: Under standard assumptions (bounded rewards, Lipschitz continuous policy, bounded variance), PRPO converges to a stationary point of the expected reward objective. Specifically, for learning rate $\eta_{t}=O(1/\sqrt{t})$ :
checks.explanation: The proof applies an upper smoothness bound to an ascent step and then rearranges it in the direction needed for descent. The objective gap has the same reversed sign. The written step-size condition also permits positive summable sequences, which need not reach a stationary point. Finally, the preceding unbiasedness and gradient-variance premises have not been established for the normalized PRPO update.
checks.demonstration:
The sign error is visible even after granting an exact gradient. Let
$$J(\theta)=0.1+0.9\operatorname{sigmoid}(\theta),\qquad \theta_0=0.$$
This is a bounded, smooth expected reward of a binary policy. Its initial derivative is $0.225$. With $\eta=0.1$, the ascent step gives $\theta_1=0.0225$. A valid smoothness constant is $L=0.225$, and the gradient noise is zero. The printed telescoping inequality would require
$$\underbrace{\eta|J'(0)|^2}_{0.0050625}\leq
\underbrace{J(0)-J(0.0225)+\tfrac L2\eta^2|J'(0)|^2}_{-0.0050053333},$$
which is impossible.

Separately, $\eta_t=t^{-2}$ satisfies the stated $O(t^{-1/2})$ upper bound. For exact ascent on $J(\theta)=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\theta)$ from zero, every iterate obeys $0\leq\theta_t\leq\tfrac14\sum_{k\geq1}k^{-2}=\pi^2/24$. The derivative therefore stays bounded away from zero. This tests the claimed sufficiency of the written schedule class; it is not an asserted trajectory of the incompletely specified PRPO implementation.
checks.repair:
State the assumptions for the actual gradient estimator and use the lower smoothness bound appropriate to ascent. If $J$ is $L$-smooth, $J\leq J_{\max}$, $\mathbb E[g_t\mid\theta_t]=\nabla J(\theta_t)$ and $\mathbb E[\|g_t-\nabla J\|^2\mid\theta_t]\leq v$, then for a constant step with $\eta L\leq1$,
$$\mathbb E[J(\theta_{t+1})-J(\theta_t)]\geq
\frac\eta2\mathbb E\|\nabla J(\theta_t)\|^2-\frac{L\eta^2v}{2}.$$
Summation yields
$$\min_{t<T}\mathbb E\|\nabla J(\theta_t)\|^2\leq
\frac{2(J_{\max}-J(\theta_0))}{\eta T}+L\eta v.$$
A horizon-dependent choice $\eta=c/\sqrt T$ gives the advertised rate under these premises. Applying this result to clipped, normalized PRPO still requires an appropriate bias or objective analysis.

checks.explanation: The separation assumption is only an upper bound. The columns may approach proportionality faster than $\varepsilon$, even when the pair is the entire Jacobian and therefore controls the full condition number exactly.
checks.demonstration:
Take
$$J_\varepsilon=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&\varepsilon^2\end{pmatrix},\qquad0<\varepsilon<1.$$
Then $c=1$, $\delta=(0,\varepsilon^2)^\top$ and $\|\delta\|=O(\varepsilon)$. There are no other columns, so the global pair-dominance premise holds with equality. But
$$\det(J_\varepsilon^\top J_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^4,\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(J_\varepsilon^\top J_\varepsilon)=2+\varepsilon^4.$$
Thus $\lambda_{\max}\to2$ and $\lambda_{\min}\sim\varepsilon^4/2$, rather than $\Theta(\varepsilon^2)$.

In general, the two-column Gram determinant is $\|j_a\|^2\|\delta_\perp\|^2$, where $\delta_\perp$ is perpendicular to $j_a$. An upper bound on $\delta$ supplies no lower bound on this determinant.
checks.repair: For the two-column claim, require $\|j_a\|=\Theta(1)$, bounded $c$, and $\|\delta_\perp\|=\Theta(\varepsilon)$. The trace is then $\Theta(1)$ and the determinant is $\Theta(\varepsilon^2)$, proving the asserted eigenvalue order. Keep the separate control of all remaining modes when transferring the result to the full Jacobian.

checks.location: Appendix B.13, General holdout RMSE ordering
checks.claim: under the Gauss–Newton linearization each summand
checks.explanation: Reducing the noise scale does not concentrate a fixed Gaussian quadratic form relative to its mean. The relative gap between the two quantities can remain constant as $\sigma\to0$, so a general strict ordering of expected MSE does not automatically become the same strict ordering of expected RMSE.
checks.demonstration:
A holdout set may contain just one off-ray point. Under the stated Gaussian linearization, its error has the form $e=\sigma\sqrt v Z$, with $v>0$ fixed and $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Therefore
$$\mathbb E[\mathrm{RMSE}]=\sigma\sqrt v\sqrt{2/\pi},\qquad
\sqrt{\mathbb E[\mathrm{MSE}]}=\sigma\sqrt v.$$
Their ratio is $\sqrt{2/\pi}$ for every $\sigma>0$, rather than tending to one.

A useful valid replacement is available. For every centered Gaussian error vector $e$,
$$\sqrt{2/\pi}\sqrt{\mathbb E\|e\|_2^2}\leq\mathbb E\|e\|_2\leq\sqrt{\mathbb E\|e\|_2^2}.$$
For the lower bound, diagonalize its covariance, divide its eigenvalues by their sum, and use concavity of the square root to bound $\sqrt{\sum_i w_iZ_i^2}\geq\sum_iw_i|Z_i|$. Jensen gives the upper bound. Dividing by the square root of the holdout size gives the corresponding RMSE bounds.
checks.repair: Use these comparability inequalities wherever the independently established MSE ratio diverges: the expected-RMSE ratio then diverges as well. For a finite strict gap, prove the expected Gaussian-norm comparison directly, supply a stronger covariance condition such as positive-semidefinite ordering, or state the conclusion for root expected MSE. The comparability bounds alone do not transfer every finite-gap ordering.
checks.scope: The small-noise expectation interchange is false. The corrected inequalities preserve conclusions based on a diverging MSE ratio; this calculation does not establish a reversal between the paper's actual designs.
checks.title: Small noise does not interchange expected RMSE and root expected MSE

checks.contextAfter: Cross-backbone hyperparameter scaling. Our central $\beta$ values work directly on Gemma-2B (80K training steps) and Mistral-7B (20K steps), but the Qwen-4B checkpoint (also 20K steps) requires a larger $\beta=3.0$ to cross the override threshold. The magnitude account predicts this shift: Qwen’s generated adapter has measurably smaller per-layer Frobenius norm (max $s_{l}\approx 0.27$ vs $\approx 1.0$ for Gemma), so a proportionally larger multiplier is required to reach the same effective margin. checks.demonstration:
For a finite matrix \(\delta\), the constrained problem is feasible exactly when \(b\in\operatorname{im}\delta^{\top}\). Under that condition, the minimum-norm solution is \(c=(\delta^{\top})^+b\), and its squared norm is \(b^{\top}(\delta^{\top}\delta)^+b\). Without feasibility, the pseudoinverse quadratic form stays finite while the constrained minimum has an empty feasible set.
Take the two-node one-edge graph with scalar orthogonal restriction maps \(F_u=1\), \(F_v=-1\). These are allowed even in the flat bundle setting. Up to orientation, \(\delta=(1\ \ 1)\), \(L_{\mathcal F}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), and \(b=(1,-1)^{\top}\). Then \(L_{\mathcal F}^+b=0\), so Definition 4.1 gives zero. But \(\delta^{\top}c=(c,c)^{\top}\neq b\) for every scalar \(c\). Definition D.1 is infeasible, so the asserted equivalence fails.

review-neurips-2026-150671.title: Federated Learning by Utility-Constrained Stochastic Aggregation for Improving Rational Participation

checks.claim: Random mixtures make simultaneously infeasible deterministic participation constraints feasible.
checks.explanation: The mixture mean is itself an admissible deterministic simplex vector. Thus whenever the mixture satisfies all thresholds through \(u_k(\alpha_k)\), that same \(\alpha\) is a deterministic feasible witness. If the constraint instead uses expected utility across candidate rows, concavity gives the displayed inequality for every client simultaneously. Randomization cannot enlarge feasibility over the unrestricted deterministic simplex under either of these criteria.
checks.demonstration:
Indeed,
\[
\alpha_k\ge0,\qquad \sum_k\alpha_k=\sum_i s_i\sum_kR_{ik}=\sum_i s_i=1.
\]
Consequently \(u_k(\alpha_k)\ge\gamma_k\) for every client is already a deterministic feasible solution. Even if \(R\) is random, Jensen gives \(u_k(\mathbb E\alpha_k)\ge\mathbb E u_k(\alpha_k)\), so averaging does not evade the conclusion. Column balance only restricts available mixtures further.

A genuine positive Jensen gap remains possible: take \(N=n_s=2\), \(R=I_2\), \(s=(1/2,1/2)\), and \(u_k(r)=1-(r-1/2)^2\). Then each candidate-average utility is \(3/4\), while the deterministic mean \(\alpha=(1/2,1/2)\) gives utility \(1\). The surplus is real relative to the candidate-average lower bound; it is not a surplus over every deterministic choice.
checks.repair: State the proved comparison with the candidate-average utility surrogate, or identify a particular deterministic baseline and establish a gain against it. The Jensen calculation supports those interpretations without claiming that an empty simplex feasibility set becomes nonempty. A feasibility-enlargement result would require a genuinely different admissible deterministic decision set or participation criterion and a proof for that changed model.
checks.scope: The finding concerns Section 3.5’s existential feasibility comparison under scalar concave utilities and an unrestricted deterministic aggregation simplex. The mixture mean is already a deterministic feasible witness.
checks.title: A feasible mixture already gives a feasible deterministic aggregate
checks.whyItMatters: The proposed explanation for participation gains confuses a surrogate-utility improvement with enlargement of the feasible set.
checks.claimContext: FedUCA uses a nonnegative strategy matrix \(R\), whose rows sum to one, and a simplex mixture \(s\). Client \(k\) evaluates its scalar aggregation weight \(\alpha_k=\sum_i s_iR_{ik}\) through a concave utility \(u_k\). Section 3.5 says that the Jensen surplus can satisfy simultaneous participation thresholds when a single deterministic aggregation vector cannot.

checks.claim: Binding weightedutility equality forces displayed componentwise proportionalutility values.
checks.explanation: A scalar equality \(s^\top v=c\) fixes only one projection of the utility vector. It allows \(v=cs/\|s\|_2^2+w\) for every \(w\perp s\); the optimization penalizes slack, not the norm of \(v\). The conclusion fails at an actual globally optimal strategy matrix, with strictly concave utilities and thresholds obtained from a common prior aggregate.
checks.demonstration:
Set \(N=n_s=2\), \(s=(3/4,1/4)\), \(u_1(r)=u_2(r)=1-(r-4/5)^2\), and \(\gamma=(1,16/25)\). These thresholds equal the utilities at the common prior simplex vector \((4/5,1/5)\). Every balanced matrix has the form
\[
R(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x&1-x\\1-x&x\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first deficit is
\[
D_1(x)=\frac34(x-\tfrac45)^2+\frac14(1-x-\tfrac45)^2
=(x-\tfrac{13}{20})^2+\frac{27}{400}>0.
\]
At its unique minimizer \(x=13/20\), the second weighted utility is \(337/400>16/25\), so \(t_2=0\). Hence this also globally minimizes the full objective, with \(t_1=27/400\). The first client’s actual component utilities and claimed values are respectively
\[
\left(\frac{391}{400},\frac{319}{400}\right),
\qquad
\left(\frac{1119}{1000},\frac{373}{1000}\right),
\]
although their weighted utility is correctly \(373/400=\gamma_1-t_1\). Equal utility components with uniform \(s\) are a positive case where the proportional formula happens to agree.
checks.repair: Retain the binding scalar equality and remove its componentwise inference. To obtain that particular vector one would additionally need to prove that the feasible utility vector lies in \(\operatorname{span}(s)\), or introduce a compatible minimum-norm utility-space selection rule and prove attainability. Neither follows from the slack objective. The valid positive-slack/binding dichotomy can be proved directly by reducing any nonbinding positive slack; the separate uniqueness conclusion under all-positive slacks is not refuted by this example.
checks.scope: The componentwise conclusion of Proposition 3.1 does not follow from its binding weighted sum. The slack dichotomy and conditional strict-concavity uniqueness statement remain separate conclusions.
checks.title: A binding weighted sum does not determine every utility component
checks.whyItMatters: Later arguments use utility components that are not implied by the optimizer’s constraints.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 3.1 sets \(\epsilon=0\) and minimizes \(\frac12\|t\|_2^2\) subject to \(R\ge0\), row sums one, column sums \(n_s/N\), \(t\ge0\), and \(\sum_i s_i u_k(R_{ik})\ge\gamma_k-t_k\). In its positive-slack case it infers a componentwise proportional utility formula from the binding scalar equality.

checks.claim: Every optimizer-based Jensen gap vanishes asdelta grows.
checks.explanation: Strict concavity does not make a zero-slack optimizer unique. An admissible optimizer selection can keep distinct rows even as the mixture becomes uniform. The example below has strictly interior strategies, common-prior thresholds, and binding constraints for every mixture.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(N=n_s=2\), \(u_1(r)=u_2(r)=1-(r-1/2)^2\), \(\epsilon=0\), and \(\gamma_1=\gamma_2=15/16\). The common prior \((1/4,3/4)\) generates these thresholds. For every \(s\), select
\[
R^*(s)=\begin{pmatrix}1/4&3/4\\3/4&1/4\end{pmatrix},\qquad t^*=0.
\]
All row utilities equal \(15/16\), so both constraints bind. Objective zero proves global optimality. Writing \(s=(S,1-S)\) gives
\[
J_k(s)=\frac14S(1-S),\qquad
S\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\delta,\delta),\qquad
\mathbb E J_k=\frac{\delta}{8(2\delta+1)}\longrightarrow\frac1{16}.
\]
The selection is constant and measurable, so no discontinuity or irregular selection is involved. The all-uniform matrix is another zero-slack optimizer with zero gap; the two optimizers cannot be assigned the same universal limiting gap.
checks.repair: A sufficient additional condition for client \(k\) is \(\gamma_k\ge u_k(1/N)\) at the uniform-mixture limit. By column balance and Jensen, every client’s averaged utility there is at most \(u_k(1/N)\), and the equal-row matrix attains all these maxima simultaneously. If client \(k\)’s column differs from \(1/N\), strict concavity gives a strictly larger positive deficit than its componentwise minimum. Thus every optimizer must have that column constant. Compactness and continuity then force its gap to zero along any sequence of optimizing matrices with \(s\to\mathbf1/n_s\); concentration and boundedness give the expected limit. Applying the condition to every client rescues the joint conclusion. A separately proved optimizer-selection rule converging to equal rows is another sufficient repair. Merely assuming binding constraints is not enough. The small-concentration limit and continuity for a fixed bounded measurable selection remain separate valid properties.
checks.scope: The finding concerns the large-concentration limit for the optimizer selections permitted by Proposition 3.2, including binding zero-slack constraints.
checks.title: Optimal strategies can retain a nonzero gap at large concentration
checks.whyItMatters: The stated concentration parameter behavior depends on optimizer selection or additional threshold conditions.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 3.2 takes strictly concave continuous utilities and a strategy matrix obtained by the balanced slack optimization. For \(s\sim\operatorname{Dir}(\delta,\ldots,\delta)\), it asserts that the expected Jensen gap vanishes as \(\delta\to\infty\). The appendix additionally describes binding utility constraints, without requiring positive optimal slacks.

checks.claim: Constant selected-client column can prioritize any individually attainableutility while preservingRconstraints.
checks.explanation: A constant column is pinned to the uniform client weight. Individual attainability elsewhere in \([0,1]\) does not imply attainability at \(1/N\), and changing other columns cannot change the selected column sum. The issue can arise after a genuine globally optimal update and with thresholds generated by a common prior.
checks.demonstration:
Take \(N=n_s=2\), \(s=(3/4,1/4)\), \(u_1(r)=1-(r-9/10)^2\), \(u_2(r)=1-(r-1/10)^2\), and \(\gamma_1=\gamma_2=1\), obtained from prior weights \((9/10,1/10)\). For
\[
R(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x&1-x\\1-x&x\end{pmatrix},
\]
both utility deficits are
\[
D(x)=\frac34(x-\tfrac9{10})^2+\frac14(1-x-\tfrac9{10})^2
=(x-\tfrac7{10})^2+\frac3{25}.
\]
The unique optimum is \(x=7/10\), with \(t=(3/25,3/25)\) and realized weights \((3/5,2/5)\). Each realized utility is \(91/100<1\), so fallback triggers. Client 1 needs weight \(9/10\), and client 2 needs \(1/10\), whereas a constant column must use \(1/2\), giving either utility only \(21/25\). All entries and prior weights are strictly interior.
checks.repair: If a selected client satisfies \(u_k(1/N)\ge\gamma_k\), the all-uniform matrix is a valid fallback; a selection rule using this condition must also prove that such a client exists. Otherwise explicitly relax column balance for the fallback update. For \(N>1\), put the chosen attainable weight \(r_k\) in every row and give each other client \((1-r_k)/(N-1)\); every row remains nonnegative and sums to one, and the selected client participates. This repairs the one-client fallback guarantee for that changed feasible set. Any subsequent bound using column balance must account for the exceptional update. The separately conditional convergence theorem does not acquire an unconditional participation guarantee merely from this construction.
checks.scope: The fallback cannot promise an arbitrary attainable client weight while preserving column balance. The convergence theorem remains conditional on a positive participation cohort.
checks.title: Column balance prevents the proposed fallback from choosing any attainable weight
checks.whyItMatters: The asserted mechanism for avoiding a zero-participant round is not guaranteed under the retained balance constraint.
checks.claimContext: Section 3.3 invokes fallback when every client fails its utility threshold. It chooses a client and sets its strategy column to a constant \(R_{ik}=r_k\), chosen to meet that client’s threshold, while saying that the remaining mass can preserve the aggregation constraints. Those constraints include \(\sum_iR_{ik}=n_s/N\).

checks.claim: The displayed contrastive loss trains paired embeddings closer and negative embeddings farther apart.
checks.explanation: Minimizing the contrastive ratio pushes paired similarities apart.

review-neurips-2026-152750.title: Norm Anchors Make Model Edits Last

checks.claim: Norm anchoring yields bounded expected weight norm for an unbounded edit stream.
checks.explanation: Norm anchoring controls the new value vector, but it does not guarantee the uniform restoring drift needed for an infinite-horizon bound. A finite-range fit also gives no bound on the recurrence's error at later edits.
checks.demonstration:
Use the paper's exact rank-one update with \(C=I\), a row matrix \(W_0=(3,4)\), and target value \(v_n^{\mathrm{new}}=2\). At each step choose a unit key \(k_n\) perpendicular to \(W_{n-1}\). The pre-edit value is then \(W_{n-1}k_n=0\), so the update is
\[W_n=W_{n-1}+2k_n^\top.\]
Orthogonality gives
\[\|W_n\|_F^2=\|W_{n-1}\|_F^2+4=25+4n.\]
Every target has the required anchored norm, and every key has norm one. Nevertheless, the weight norm diverges. This sequence violates the positive-slope scaling fitted in the experiments; it shows why that scaling must be an additional uniform premise, rather than a consequence of anchoring.
checks.repair:
State a uniform condition that produces negative drift. For example, with unit keys and the history \(\mathcal F_{n-1}\), assume
\[\mathbb E[k_nk_n^\top\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]\succeq aI,\qquad a>0.\]
Then the exact update with target norm \(\tau\) yields
\[\mathbb E\|W_n\|_F^2\leq(1-a)\mathbb E\|W_{n-1}\|_F^2+\tau^2,\]
and hence a bound by \(\max\{\mathbb E\|W_0\|_F^2,\tau^2/a\}\). Alternatively, present the affine recurrence as a finite-range explanatory model and remove the unconditional infinite-horizon conclusion.
checks.scope: The issue is the inference from anchoring and finite-range fits to boundedness for an unbounded sequence. The conditional stable recurrence is valid when its uniform assumptions hold. The counterexample does not contradict the measured model-editing results.
checks.title: A fixed target norm does not by itself bound an unlimited edit sequence
checks.claimContext: Corollary 3.3 concludes that the expected squared weight norm remains bounded as the number of edits tends to infinity. Its approximate recurrence uses the affine scaling of pre-edit value norms fitted in Appendix B.4. The appendix explicitly limits that fit and its positive slope to the observed range.

checks.location: Appendix B.3 proof of Theorem 3, Step 3 (Eq. (6)); Theorem 3 statement, work/text/153421.txt lines 152, 749-767
checks.claim: NMD is positively homogeneous of degree 1 in the single variable u_m, so Euler's theorem gives u_m^T grad_{u_m} NMD = NMD, which makes P_{u_m} = I - u_m grad NMD^T / NMD idempotent (a projection matrix).
checks.explanation: Scaling every deviation by $c>0$ multiplies each pairwise distance by $c$. Scaling only $u_m$ does not: $\|u_m-u_n\|$ is a distance from the fixed point $u_n$, and pairs excluding $m$ do not change at all. The joint Euler identity therefore cannot justify Equation (6)'s separate identity for each behavior, or the claimed idempotency of each $P_{u_m}$.
checks.demonstration:
Write $N(U)$ for the unscaled empirical diversity in the denominator of Equation (4), with $U$ stacking all behavior deviations. Under the shared-covariance Gaussian and linear-mean assumptions, it is a positive multiple of the sum of pairwise distances. Consequently, $N(cU)=cN(U)$ for $c>0$, but scaling only one behavior does not scale distances from the other fixed behaviors by the same factor.

Take two one-dimensional Gaussian behaviors with shared variance $1$ and constant feature $\phi=(1,0)^\top$. Rank-one LoRA factors can produce deviations $u_1=1$ and $u_2=3$ at every observation, with zero shared mean. The empirical normalization for two behaviors gives $N=|u_1-u_2|=2$, differentiable in an open neighborhood of this example. Thus $\partial_{u_1}N=-1$ and $\partial_{u_2}N=1$. In particular, $u_1\partial_{u_1}N=-1\ne2$, contradicting Equation (6).

The scalar matrices in Theorem 3 are $P_{u_1}=1-1(-1)/2=3/2$ and $P_{u_2}=1-3(1)/2=-1/2$. Neither is idempotent: each satisfies $P_{u_m}^2-P_{u_m}=3/4$. Nor does the first block annihilate the diversity derivative, since $(\partial_{u_1}N)P_{u_1}=-3/2$. All covariance, linearity and local differentiability conditions hold. The correct Euler identity is the joint one, $\sum_m u_m^\top\nabla_{u_m}N=N$, including all observation blocks if more than one observation is used.
checks.repair:
State the result for the full coupled normalization map. Stack every deviation into $U$, let $v=\nabla_U N(U)$, and define $\alpha=N_{\mathrm{des}}/N(U)$ and $Z=Z_{\mathrm{shared}}+\alpha U$. Joint homogeneity gives $v^\top U=N(U)$, so
$$J=\frac{\partial Z}{\partial U}=\alpha P,\qquad P=I-\frac{Uv^\top}{N(U)},\qquad P^2=P,\qquad v^\top P=0.$$
This is a genuine joint oblique projection. Its diagonal blocks are the paper's individual matrices, but the off-diagonal blocks $-u_m(\nabla_{u_n}N)^\top/N$ are essential; a diagonal block of an idempotent matrix need not itself be idempotent.

For a differentiable total reward, the complete chain rule is $\nabla_U R=\alpha P^\top\nabla_ZR$. The transpose cannot generally be removed because $P$ is not symmetric. The same normalization also gives $N(Z-Z_{\mathrm{shared}})=N_{\mathrm{des}}$ exactly, wherever the denominator is positive. Thus the corrected theorem preserves the architecture's diversity constraint and describes reward optimization within that constrained family. It does not assert that the constraint leaves the unconstrained reward maximum unchanged.

For the example, $P=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3/2&-1/2\\3/2&-1/2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is idempotent and satisfies $(-1,1)P=0$. This verifies the repair while leaving the per-behavior projection claim false.
checks.scope: Equation (6) and the per-behavior idempotency claim in Theorem 3 are false. Under the stated Gaussian and linear assumptions, the joint Jacobian $\alpha P$ gives the corrected diversity-preserving derivative wherever $N(U)>0$ and $N$ is differentiable. This repairs the projection description, without asserting that constrained reward optimization attains the unconstrained optimum.

checks.claim: Because the squashed action distribution is the 1-Lipschitz (tanh) push-forward of the pre-activation Gaussian, pre-activation NMD upper-bounds action-space NMD and the relative ordering of pairwise behavior distances is preserved.
checks.explanation: Two distances can contract by different factors. An upper bound on each distance cannot establish their ordering after the nonlinear map, even when all means are close to zero.
checks.demonstration: In one dimension, compare equal-variance Gaussian pairs with means \((0.1,0.11005)\) and \((0,0.01)\), and common standard deviation \(\sigma=10^{-6}\). Their pre-activation \(W_2\) distances are \(0.01005>0.01\). At zero variance the action distances are approximately \(0.0099398752<0.0099996667\). Each positive-variance action distance differs from its zero-variance value by at most \(2\sigma\): couple each Gaussian to its mean and use that \(\tanh\) is 1-Lipschitz. The reversal margin exceeds \(4\sigma\), so the reversal remains strict for these nondegenerate Gaussians. The mechanism can be placed arbitrarily close to zero: compare gaps \(h(1+a^2/2)\) near \(a>0\) and \(h\) near zero, take \(h=o(a)\), and use \(\tanh\prime(a)=1-a^2+O(a^4)\); then choose sufficiently small positive variance.
checks.repair: Retain the valid upper-bound statement. A sufficient ranking condition needs both lower and upper distortion bounds: if the common support lies in \([-M,M]^d\), then \(\ell=\operatorname{sech}^2M\) and \(L=1\) give \(\ell W_2(P,Q)\le W_2(\tanh_\#P,\tanh_\#Q)\le LW_2(P,Q)\). Thus a smaller distance \(d_1\) remains smaller than \(d_2\) if \(Ld_1<\ell d_2\). Gaussian laws have unbounded support, so applying such a bounded-region argument to them additionally requires explicit tail error bounds.
checks.scope: The contraction inequality and approximate linear behavior near zero are valid. The unsupported conclusion is exact relative-order preservation without a margin or lower distortion hypothesis.

Detectors are then ranked by this average error in each patch, and a reward of $1$ is assigned to the top-k detector, while the remaining detectors receive $0$ .

checks.contextAfter: We first examine the impact of the low-confidence threshold in the DAEDAL baseline. As shown in Table 5, the performance of DAEDAL is highly sensitive to this threshold. A lower threshold (e.g., 0.1 or 0.2) makes the model conservative in expanding the length, failing to correct underestimated lengths (e.g., $L=4$ ). checks.contextAfter: Density ratio estimation lies at the core of many GAN variants (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Nowozin et al., 2016). In classic GANs, the discriminator implicitly estimates the density ratio between the data and model distributions. However, in high-dimensional image modeling, both distributions typically concentrate on low-dimensional manifolds and are not absolutely continuous, making the density ratio—and consequently the Jensen–Shannon divergence—ill-defined. This issue is widely recognized as a major source of GAN training instability (Arjovsky & Bottou, 2017; Arjovsky et al., 2017; Mescheder et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2017).

Use \(N=2048\), with \(1638\) excitatory and \(410\) inhibitory columns. Choose an excitatory neuron \(r\) in the recurrent-driven population. Define a matrix \(W_0\) whose excitatory entries are \(1/N\), whose inhibitory entries are \(-1/N\), and whose inhibitory entries in row \(r\) are instead \(-8/N\). Every column obeys Dale's sign constraint and every magnitude is positive.

This matrix has rank at most two. Its nonzero eigenvalues are those of
\[B=\begin{pmatrix}1228/2048&1/2048\\-2870/2048&0\end{pmatrix}.\]
Let \(\rho\approx0.5984660163\) be its spectral radius and put \(W=W_0/\rho\), as in Algorithm 1's normalization. Then \(\rho(W)=1\), while row \(r\) sums to
\[\frac{1638-8\cdot410}{2048\rho}\approx-1.33968812.\]
With \(h_0=0\), zero bias, softplus activation and \(\alpha=1/2\), this recurrent-driven neuron receives no external input. Equation (S5) gives

The inequality is strict and persists under small perturbations of the positive magnitudes, so it is not confined to a single zero-probability Gaussian initialization. \[P_A=(0.2601,0.2499,0.245,0.245),\qquad P_B=(0.258,0.342,0.2,0.2).\]
Under \(A\), the positive item outranks every negative, so \(\mathrm{AUC}(A)=1\). Under \(B\), it loses to \(01\) and beats the other two negatives, so \(\mathrm{AUC}(B)=2/3\).

There are \(n\) weights, each at most one. If even one were smaller than one, their sum would be smaller than \(n\). Thus the mass constraint with \(K=n\) uniquely determines the all-ones vector.

The printed threshold search actually reaches this outcome. Set \(m=n-1\); its formula gives \(\lambda=x_{(n)}\), satisfying \(x_{(n-1)}\ge\lambda\ge x_{(n)}\). Every logit obeys \(x_i\ge\lambda\), so
\[w_i=\min\{1,e^{(x_i-\lambda)/\tau}\}=1,\qquad\bar w_i=\frac{nw_i}{\sum_jw_j}=1.\]
For a concrete allowed rank window, take normalized ranks \((0,1/2,1)\), anchor zero, logits \((0,-1/2,-1)\), and \(\tau=1/2\). A supplied mass \(K=1\) is overwritten by three; \(m=2\), \(\lambda=-1\) gives \(w=(1,1,1)\). Algorithm 2 returns the original negative advantages.

Keep \(n=|\mathcal N|\) as a separate count and preserve the requested mass \(K\). Use \(n\) for rank normalization and array limits, and use \(K\) in the mass constraint. For \(\tau>0\) and \(0<K<n\), retain the already correct main-text formula
\[\lambda=\tau\log\!\left(\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}e^{x_{(i)}/\tau}\right)-\tau\log(K-m),\qquad m<K,\]

\[\sum_iw_i=m+e^{-\lambda/\tau}\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}e^{x_{(i)}/\tau}=K.\]

\[w=\frac{(1,e^{-1},e^{-2})}{1+e^{-1}+e^{-2}},\]
